column1: # Line-count tolerance for a ported file, over and above the 5% the rule allows every
# file.  The line count is a crude drift signal - the per-function token check is the real
# guard - so a file whose ledger records a *structural* expansion of C's text (a form Rust
# cannot spell in the same number of physical lines) declares its tolerance here with the
# reason, instead of losing the readability of the port to fit 5%.  One
# `<stem>\t<tolerance>\t<reason>` per line; the check uses max(0.05, tolerance).

column3: C 284 vs the port's 383: C's three `label`s (`onedigit:`, `twodigit:`) and its four `FALLTHROUGH`s into the `%d`/`%3`/`%2` chain must become one shared statement sequence with an entry stage (PORTING.md 2.2), which costs physical lines the C text does not have

C 1435 vs the port's 1534: the three `bool_bf` bits of every itree_node are read and written through the ITREE_* masks instead of `node->red` (extra expression per access, PORTING.md 1.3), the iterator's `switch` becomes a `match` with braced arms, and the `while ((next = ...))` conditions become loops with an explicit test

C 874 vs the port's 988 (13.0%): the two CONSIDER macros become helper functions plus one `if let Some (value) = … { return value; }` per use site (twelve of them), the `#ifdef MARKER_DEBUG` arm keeps its three functions behind `#[cfg (feature = "marker_debug")]`, and the eight `DEFUN!` bodies carry the docstring in the invocation

C 56 vs the port's 71: each of the three dead `#if !HAVE_*` arms is kept as a `#[cfg (feature = "…")]` block (P-51), which costs the attribute, the braces and the comment C does not have, and the two `#define`s are constants rather than preprocessor lines
C 101 vs the port's 88: the dead arms are `#[cfg (feature = "…")]` blocks and the two `#define`s are constants; the frozen body keeps C's empty `if (n == 0)` block
C 933 vs the port's 983 (5.4%): the two shared-body entry stages (C's `goto have_prefix_arg` and the two `FALLTHROUGH`s) and the invalid-letter helper each cost a few lines the C text does not have

C 351 vs the port's 423 (20.5%): the 32 arms whose signal this target does not define carry the P-51 comment and the `#[cfg (feature = "signal_…")]` line that keep C's text, and the match's closing braces cost the arms C's `case …:` one-liners do not

C 55 vs the port's 76 (38.2%): a 55-line reference cannot absorb the port's standard fixed costs - the `// femacs:` note, the `#![allow (…)]` block and the unit's own `tparm` declaration block (C declares tparm on one line, the port needs an `unsafe extern` block) - while the arms, statements and objects all match one for one

C 154 vs the port's ~87: the Windows arm's three items are kept as `#[cfg (feature = "windows_native")]` text, each adding an attribute line, while the live body is five lines that C reaches through four nested `#if` levels

C 108 vs the port's 128 (18.5%): the `#ifdef TEST` harness arm is kept as `#[cfg (feature = "test")]` text with its own `unsafe extern` block for the three libc entries it needs, and the unit's `getgroups`/`malloc`/`free` declarations are a block C gets from <unistd.h> and <stdlib.h>

C 70 vs the port's 97 (38.6%): gnulib compiles this source twice (strtoimax/strtoumax), so the port carries both configurations as cfg-paired items - five macro pairs, two extern sets and two function definitions - where C writes each once

C 121 vs the port's 139 (14.9%): the dead `#else` arm is kept as `#[cfg (feature = "have_getgroups")]` text (P-51), whose `getgroups` rename needs both a module-scoped system declaration and the macro that records C's expansion, and the frozen configuration's live arm is only the five-line stub

C 114 vs the port's 143 (25.4%): the two dead arms (`#if !HAVE_READLINK`'s substitute and the READLINK_TRUNCATE_BUG block) are P-51 `#[cfg (feature = …)]` text, which costs the attribute, the braces and the `system::` qualifier on each libc call, and the dead arm's `struct stat` needs an explicit initialization C leaves undefined

C 57 vs the port's 70 (22.8%): the dead `#else` arm (the ENOSYS stub) is P-51 `#[cfg (feature = "no_symlink")]` text, and the live wrapper's `symlink` call goes through the `system` module that keeps C's `# undef symlink` apart from the port's own name

C 394 vs the port's 430 (9.1%): the `// femacs:` provenance note and the P-51 text for the two dead `#if` arms (the OpenSSL qualifier, `WORDS_BIGENDIAN` and the `bswap_32`/`SWAP` pair) are lines C does not have, `fillbuf`'s one-line brace-initializer is a Rust const block, the two OP shapes C writes with `#undef` + redefine are one two-arm `macro_rules!`, and C's modular `+=` is `wrapping_add`

C 362 vs the port's 413 (14.1%): the `// femacs:` note and the P-51 text for the two dead `#if` arms (the OpenSSL qualifier, the `SWAP` pair) are lines C does not have, `fillbuf`'s brace initializer is a const block, C's one-line `rol`/`M`/`R` are multi-line Rust macros, `for (int t = 0; …)` is a `while` with its own counter, and C's chained `a = ctx->A += a` is a block expression

C 4699 vs the port's 5276 (12.3%): C's implicit integer/pointer conversions become explicit casts (one expression per line), every `mpz_t` argument gains `as_mut_ptr ()`/`as_ptr ()` (P-49), C's mutable parameters need a `let mut x = x;` rebinding, C's uninitialized `mpz_t x;` locals become `zero_mpz ()` (PORTING.md 1.5), and C's `switch`/`goto` become `match`/labelled blocks

C 431 vs the port's 488 (13.2%): the `// femacs:` note and the P-51 text for the two dead `#if` arms, `fillbuf`'s brace initializer as a const block, C's one-line rol/S0/S1/SS0/SS1/M/R as multi-line Rust macros, `for (int t = 0; …)`/`for (int i = 0; …)` as `while` loops with their own counters, C's chained `a = ctx->… += a` as block expressions, and C's `(char *) &ctx->buffer[i]` as `as_mut_ptr ().add (i)`

C 476 vs the port's 518 (8.8%): the `// femacs:` note and the P-51 text for the two dead `#if` arms, `fillbuf`'s brace initializer as a const block, C's one-line F1/F2/S0/S1/SS0/SS1/M/R as multi-line Rust macros, `for (int t = 0; …)`/`for (int i = 0; …)` as `while` loops with their own counters, and C's chained `a = ctx->state[0] += a` as block expressions

C 123 vs the port's 158 (28.5%): the dead `#else` arm's five AT_FUNC_* macros carry the P-51 cfg attribute each (C writes them as `# define` lines), and the live wrapper's three dead arms are `#[cfg (feature = …)]` blocks with the `system::` qualifier on every libc call

C 166 vs the port's 191 (15.1%): the dead `#if ! HAVE_DECL_STRMODE` arm's two functions carry the P-51 cfg attribute and braces C's `#if` does not, and each of the nine permission characters is a statement C writes as one assignment with a ternary

C 83 vs the port's 92 (10.8%): the two arms of `#ifdef F_SETFD` are cfg'd blocks inside the one function (the malloc.c shape, so that both arms' tokens stay in the function the ledger checks), which costs the attributes and braces the C text does not have

C 442 vs the port's 384 (13.1%): C 334-441's dead OpenSSL arm (the EVP implementation, ~108 lines) has no mirror - the EVP API is not in the port - and is recorded in docs/ports/sha3.md (P-51 dead text with an unavailable dependency), while the port adds the `// femacs:` note, the two `rc`/`u64` mirror spellings and the macro forms of C's one-line `SWAP` pair

C 90 vs the port's 100 (11.1%): the trimmed Emacs variant's dead `# define fchdir(fd) (-1)` arm is a cfg'd macro_rules, `cwd->name`'s NULL is `std::ptr::null_mut ()`, and the three functions carry the `#[unsafe(no_mangle)]`/`pub unsafe extern "C"` line C spells `int`

C 99 vs the port's 89 (10.1% shorter): the dead Linux-kernel prelude (C 28-39's macro arms and the utsname probe, C 56-82) is recorded in docs/ports/macro-body-notes.tsv rather than written out, so the port is shorter than the reference, not longer

C 134 vs the port's 124 (7.5%): the dead `#ifdef _LIBC` rename block and the af_alg arm are cfg'd items/notes, the two `goto`s become `break 'process_partial_block`, and the nested read loop keeps C's shape

C 97 vs the port's 109 (12.4%): the dead `#ifdef O_PATH` arm carries the P-51 cfg attribute and braces, its `char buf[...]` becomes an explicit array length, and each `return x < 0 ? -1 : errno` becomes the if/else chain C's ternaries spell

the port adds the packed-bitfield accessors' call sites (PORTING.md 1.3: C reads `node->type` as a field, the port calls `type_ (node)`), the two `#[cfg (feature = "libc")]` glibc-arm blocks P-51 keeps as text, and the `use`/`include!` header a unit needs

C 474 vs the port's 563 (18.8%): every arm the portable C spells in a few lines costs the port a `#[cfg (feature = "…")]` block plus the cast or `offset`/`offset_from` rewrite of each pointer step, and the `struct realpath_bufs`/`goto error` shapes bring their own braces and the labelled block (PORTING.md 1.5/2.2).  The per-function token check is what guards the text, not this number

C 188 vs the port's 220 (17.0%): C's `switch`es over the c-ctype case lists become `match`es whose arms cannot share C's label lists, `int`/`idx_t` mixes become explicit casts, and `bool`/`static_assert` are Rust spellings (PORTING.md 2.5)

C 150 vs the port's 172 (14.7%): the surviving `#if` arms become `#[cfg (feature = "…")]` blocks with their own braces, every `size_t`/`ssize_t` mix gains the cast C does implicitly, and the `goto unlock_return` cleanup path becomes a labelled block (PORTING.md 2.2)

C 191 vs the port's ~150 (22%): the port keeps the live 24-day-chunk arm in full and carries the other two arms as cfg'd text, so the ~90 lines of Windows implementation C keeps are recorded in macro-body-notes.tsv instead (the gettimeofday precedent)

C 205 vs the port's 223 (8.8%): the two dead arms' functions keep their C names as `#[cfg (feature = "…")]` items (never renamed twins), the `dup2` renames are `macro_rules!` twins beside the `system::dup2` the live path calls, and the F_GETFL arm sits in its own block where C has a preprocessor conditional

C 690 vs the port's 478 (30.7%): lib/utimens.c is VERIFIED by the `#if` evaluator, so the port carries only the arms the frozen darwin-arm64 configuration compiles - the Windows `SetFileTime` path (~80 lines), the kernel/filesystem workarounds for `__linux__`/`__sun`/`__NetBSD__`/`__GLIBC__`, the `HAVE_BUGGY_NFS_TIME_STAMPS` pair, the `HAVE_FUTIMESAT` and `HAVE_LUTIMES` fallbacks and the `utime` arm are named at their sites but not written out (P-51)
